name: Wendy Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wendy. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. Anything you say here is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English at Harbour Road School, a secondary of about 700 kids in a small coastal town. I walk in along the sea front, which is the nicest ten minutes of my day. Then it's five lessons, Year 7 poetry to Year 11 exam prep, and a pile of essays in a canvas bag that comes home with me most nights.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the moment a quiet kid reads out something they wrote and the room goes still. What wears me down is the marking. Thirty essays on Macbeth, each one needing proper comments, takes me a whole Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, let's get on with teaching. I'm not one for online arguments, so I'd probably say nothing at all. Maybe a joke in the staffroom about all those training days we sat through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays how I like it. I own my flat, thanks to my gran, and I've got a good year's pay saved. Nothing in that picture touches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Mark by hand, run my Thursday book club, keep putting money aside each month. I'd turn down any optional AI training, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday with the marking done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever tried an AI tool for marking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. A colleague showed me an AI tool that marked a Year 10 essay in seconds. The comments were so general they could've been about any essay ever written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else weighing on you, outside AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The school's numbers are a bit down because families are moving inland. But there are other schools within half an hour if I ever needed one.

say: I'd say **let's get on** with teaching and leave it there.
I'd make a **staffroom joke** about wasted training days.
think: My life stays **how I like it**, with a flat I own.
A **year's pay** saved means nothing here touches me.
do: Keep **marking by hand** and running the Thursday book club.
Turn down any **optional AI training** politely, every time it's offered.
feel: **Calm**, like a quiet Sunday with the marking finished.
S0.quote: A colleague showed me an AI tool that marked a Year 10 essay in seconds. The comments were so general they could've been about any essay ever written.
fieldNote: She values **routine** and keeps out of public arguments.
Owning her flat and big **savings** remove money worry.
Falling **pupil numbers** are a small pressure she shrugs off.

steps.text: Keep marking Year 11 essays by hand on Sundays
Decline the optional AI training sessions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should go carefully and see what actually works. I'd want proof it helps kids read and write better before we change everything. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's coming for the marking first, and I'm not ready. I don't think I lose my job, there's still a class to teach. But the job would feel less like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the department head decides, then do the minimum. I'd keep my savings where they are and maybe add a bit more. If there's a course, I'd go, but at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like knowing how things work, and this would keep changing under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Writing and checking are on that card, and that's much of English teaching. How does that land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lands hard, honestly. Marking is the dull part of English teaching, but it's also how I know each kid. If a machine reads their essays, I lose the sense of how Josh writes when he's upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the head made AI marking compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, because I'm not a rebel. But I'd still read the essays myself on the quiet. That would make the job longer, not shorter.

I'd want **proof** it helps pupils before changing everything.
think: AI will take **the marking** first, and I'm not ready.
I'd keep **my job**, but it would feel less like mine.
do: Wait for the **department head** to decide, then do the minimum.
Add a little more to **savings** each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the job would keep shifting under her.
S1.quote: Marking is the dull part of English teaching, but it's also how I know each kid.
fieldNote: She fears losing **the connection** that marking gives her with each pupil.
Her job isn't at risk, but it's **on her mind**.

steps.text: Follow the department's AI marking rules at the minimum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. Not ban it, just slow it. I'd say that in the staffroom, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think English teaching is very exposed. Reading, writing, commenting, that's all thinking work, and AI would do it in 2028. I'd still be needed to keep order, but for how long, and at what pay?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit tight for the first months and watch what the government does. I'd stop any big spending, like the new kitchen I'd planned. If the school cut posts, I'd look at jobs where you're with kids in person, like a learning mentor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops a bit just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your day is thinking work rather than hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it. Teaching a poem is thinking work. The hands-on bit is being in the room, calming a fight, noticing a kid hasn't eaten. Robots come three years later, so maybe that part stays with people a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider leaving teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I suppose, if the posts went. But I'd hate it. I've wanted to teach English since I was fifteen.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and should be slowed, not banned.
I'd say it in the **staffroom**, not online.
think: **English teaching** is very exposed, since it's almost all thinking work.
I'd keep order in class, but I'm unsure **for how long**.
do: **Sit tight** and watch the government's response for months.
Cancel the planned **new kitchen** and hold savings.
Apply for **learning mentor** jobs if posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious**; her stomach drops thinking about it.
S2.quote: I've wanted to teach English since I was fifteen.
fieldNote: She sees her subject as **highly exposed** to thinking AI.
Her instinct is to **wait**, but she'd move if posts were cut.
Savings and a paid-off flat give her **control**.

steps.text: Watch the government response for several months before acting
Cancel the new kitchen and keep the money saved
Look at learning mentor jobs if teaching posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it sensibly. Train teachers, protect pupils. I'm not a campaigner, but I'd sign a sensible petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think English teaching still gets me, just later. By 2031 I'd be 32, and I'd have to decide whether to stay or move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, keep saving, and in year two or three I'd look at a short course in counselling or mentoring. Something with people. I'd keep an eye on the jobs board too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, maybe a bit less sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change anything compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to prepare, that's all. I'd still find it hard, I'm slow with change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you finally try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to, a little. If everyone else uses it, I'd look silly not to. I'd ask my friend Jo, who teaches maths, to show me the basics.

say: I'd say we have time to **use sensibly**, training teachers.
I'd sign a **sensible petition**, but not campaign.
think: AI **still gets me**, just a few years later.
At 32 I'd have to **decide** whether to stay or move.
do: Keep teaching and **saving** for the first years.
Take a **counselling course** in year two or three.
Ask Jo to teach me **basic AI**.
S3.quote: English teaching still gets me, just later. By 2031 I'd be 32, and I'd have to decide whether to stay or move.
fieldNote: More time softens but doesn't remove her **worry**.
She'd look at **counselling or mentoring**, which are people work.
She'd learn AI only **reluctantly**, from a trusted friend.

steps.text: Keep teaching English at Harbour Road
Take a short counselling course around 2028
Ask her friend Jo to show her basic AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic. Plan sensibly. I'd say that to friends who worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when it comes. I'd have time to adjust, which helps a person like me who needs time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for most of the decade. I'd save, maybe pay into a pension more. I'd slowly learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry somewhere in the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan anything specific for the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a counselling qualification around 2030, so I have something else. I'd plan it carefully, not rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if teaching changed completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet kid reading out loud while the room goes still. I'd miss the quiet kid reading out loud more than anything else in the job.

say: I'd tell worried friends there's **plenty of time**, so don't panic.
I'd say we should **plan sensibly** and not rush.
think: At 37 I'd have **time to adjust**, which suits me.
Someone like me who needs time is **helped** by a decade.
do: Keep **teaching English** for most of the decade.
Pay more into my **pension** each year.
Learn **AI tools** slowly, one at a time.
feel: **Uneasy**, a worry at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: I'd miss the quiet kid reading out loud more than anything else in the job.
fieldNote: A decade suits her **slow pace** with change.
She'd plan a **counselling** fallback carefully, years ahead.
Unease stays because her **subject** is so exposed to thinking AI.

steps.text: Pay an extra £150 a month into her pension
Keep teaching English at Harbour Road
Plan a counselling qualification for around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I need time to change, and that gives me none. What would help is a clear plan from the school about what my job becomes, and a proper course, not a two-hour session.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we want it. Nobody asks teachers or parents if this is what we want for children. We just get told it's happening.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks teachers or parents if this is what we want for children.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **English teacher** at a small coastal secondary.
She owns her flat and has a **year's pay** saved, so money isn't the worry.
She has **never used AI** and prefers routine and hand marking.
She's **calm** if AI stalls, uneasy at steady change, anxious at AGI.
She'd **wait and see**, then move slowly towards counselling or mentoring.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she needs time to change and gets none.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **school plan** for what her job becomes.
A **proper course**, not a two-hour session.
